text: Kevin Hou, who leads product engineering on Google Antigravity, posted on X recommending /swarm paired with Gemini 4 Neon and Orchestrator right after a quota reset. I had seen /swarm mentioned when Gemini 4 Carbon rolled out, and I wrote about Theo letting Neon use it on ts-rust in my Gemini 4 Neon review , but I hadn’t run it myself yet. So I opened the Antigravity desktop app on this site’s repository ( flaviocopes.com ) and put it through a real audit. The main question I wanted to answer was simple: what do you need /swarm for that one good agent can’t do on its own? Before running /swarm , I picked Orchestrator in the model selector. In Antigravity, Orchestrator pairs two models inside one conversation: a larger planner model explores the codebase, writes the plan, and checks progress, while a faster executor model handles searches, file edits, builds, and tests. It is the same split I tested when running Fable as the orchestrator with Opus in Claude Code , except built into the picker. Here is how Antigravity splits the two roles on Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra plans: There is one small UI quirk when you open the model menu under the prompt box. Hovering Orchestrator opens a submenu with only the four planner models (Neon, Carbon, Argon, Claude Opus 5.5). I went looking for Hydrogen there and didn’t see it. Hydrogen isn’t listed in that submenu because it is the executor, already selected by default under Settings -> Models -> Orchestrator Settings . Clicking Orchestrator ( Gemini 4 Neon High ) directly gives you Neon High planning and Hydrogen executing. To give /swarm a real job that divides cleanly across separate parts of a repo, I asked for a strictly read-only audit of three areas of flaviocopes.com plus a verifier to check every claim: /swarm Audit three areas of flaviocopes.com with separate read-only workers: (1) scripts/check-internal-links.mjs and recent drafts for broken internal links, (2) scripts/audit-images.mjs and public/images/ for oversized or unused assets, (3) scripts/build-site.mjs and package.json for the biggest build-time bottlenecks. Have a verifier cross-check every reported file path and line number, then post one ranked summary on the board. Here is the prompt ready to go in the Antigravity app with the swarm command chip and Orchestrator selected: When you run /swarm , your main conversation becomes @coordinator . It doesn’t do the audit work itself. Instead, it spent about a minute inspecting the repo, spawned five workers ( @links-auditor , @images-auditor , @build-auditor , @verifier , and a quiet @monitor to watch for stalls), and returned an Open the Swarm UI button while the auditors ran in parallel. That right-hand Swarm pane has four tabs: Overview , Board , Members , and Graph . The Board tab is the shared message feed where the entire team communicates in public. Posts #1 through #4 are the coordinator’s briefs to each worker, spelling out what they own, what they must not touch (no edits, no writing to seo-reports/ ), and how to report back ( @verifier [done] with exact repo-relative paths and 1-based line numbers). Notice one interesting detail in the Members tab. Even though the conversation had Orchestrator Gemini 4 Neon High selected, every worker row ( @coordinator , @build-auditor , @images-auditor , @links-auditor , and @verifier ) showed gemini-4-hydrogen on the right while executing. Workers that aren’t needed yet (like @verifier at the start) sit in Standing by without burning tokens until another member mentions them on the board. Here is how the run flowed from prompt to ranked report: The Graph tab lets you inspect the swarm in two ways: a Mentions graph showing who messaged whom (with arrow counts and an Export GIF button), and a Hive view with pixel-art bees inside hexagons and a replay scrubber across every post. The Hive view is fun to watch, and the replay scrubber at the bottom is where I spotted the most useful part of the whole run. At 9:01 AM ( +9m 42s from start, post #11 of 14), @links-auditor posted a corrected report to @verifier : @verifier [done] Corrected report for #7 (fixing the two items flagged in #10; verified at 2026-11-25T08:01:17Z / 09:01:17+01:00): Counts updated for current wall-clock: 2,328 posts in... @verifier had checked @links-auditor ’s first report ( #7 ) against the actual files in the repository, caught two inaccuracies in post #10 , and sent it back to be fixed before the coordinator wrote the final report. Once all three tracks passed verification ( #13 ), the coordinator posted the 10-item ranked summary to the board ( #14 ), killed the four workers (dropping Members from 5 back to 1), and printed the same summary in the main chat. The top findings were real bugs and bottlenecks I hadn’t noticed: Every item in that list came with exact file paths, line numbers, and measured sizes, cross-checked by @verifier before I read a word of it. For most daily coding, you don’t need /swarm . One agent on Orchestrator (Neon + Hydrogen) is simpler, finishes small edits faster, and uses far less quota. Here is where /swarm earns the extra tokens: And here is where a single agent is still the better choice: Antigravity now has four ways to run multiple agents, and it helps to keep them straight: The same /swarm command also works in the Antigravity CLI ( agy ), with a live terminal board you open using /swarm board or Alt+S . (If you use Cursor or Claude Code instead of Antigravity, pstack has a separate /swarm skill that uses the same name for fanning out parallel slices.) For normal day-to-day work on flaviocopes.com and my Mac apps, I stay on a single agent with Orchestrator (Gemini 4 Neon + Hydrogen) . Most features and bug fixes touch tightly connected files and don’t justify paying 4x to 5x the quota. I would pull out /swarm for two specific jobs: It fits the same rule I use for overnight agent runs : only spin up multiple workers when the task genuinely splits into independent questions or slices, and when you know what check decides whether the result is right.
